content:
If you're living with arthritis and planning a pregnancy, or are already pregnant, there's good news: many women with arthritis have healthy pregnancies. However, careful planning with your rheumatologist is essential, particularly around medication management.

Quick answer: Managing arthritis during pregnancy requires careful planning with your rheumatologist. Some medications like methotrexate must be stopped months before conception, while others like hydroxychloroquine are considered safe. Folic acid (400 micrograms daily) should be started at least three months prior. Regular monitoring throughout pregnancy and planning for potential postpartum flares are crucial for a healthy outcome.

Before You Conceive

Ideally, speak to your rheumatology team 3-6 months before trying to conceive:

  • Some arthritis medications must be stopped well before conception
  • Your disease should be well-controlled before pregnancy — active inflammation increases risks
  • Ask your GP or hospital for a preconception counselling appointment
  • Start folic acid (400 micrograms daily) at least 3 months before conception

Medication Safety

Generally Safe During Pregnancy

  • Hydroxychloroquine — considered safe and often continued throughout
  • Sulfasalazine — generally safe but requires folic acid supplementation
  • Low-dose prednisolone — may be used for flare management
  • Paracetamol — first-line pain relief in pregnancy

Must Be Stopped Before Pregnancy

  • Methotrexate — must be stopped at least 3 months before conception (men and women)
  • Leflunomide — requires a washout period
  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — avoid after 20 weeks; discuss with doctor before 20 weeks

Discuss with Your Rheumatologist

  • Biologics — some are safer than others during pregnancy; many are stopped in the third trimester
  • JAK inhibitors — generally stopped before conception

During Pregnancy

Many women with inflammatory arthritis experience improvement during pregnancy, particularly in the second and third trimesters. However:

  • Some women experience flares, especially in the first trimester
  • Regular monitoring with both rheumatology and obstetric teams is important
  • Stay as active as possible — swimming and walking are excellent during pregnancy
  • Physiotherapy can help with joint pain and posture changes

After Birth

  • Flares are common in the first 3-6 months postpartum — plan medication restart with your team
  • Breastfeeding is possible with many arthritis medications — check each one individually
  • Ask for help at home — managing a newborn with arthritis requires support
  • Contact your rheumatology team early if symptoms worsen

UK Resources

  • UK Teratology Information Service (UKTIS) — bumps.org for medication safety data
  • NHS preconception clinics — ask your rheumatologist for a referral
  • NRAS — leaflets on RA and pregnancy

With proper planning and support from your healthcare team, arthritis need not prevent you from having a healthy pregnancy and baby.

Practical next steps for Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK

If you came here about Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Quick questions about Arthritis Pregnancy

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
